client: I lost my dad two months ago, really suddenly, and honestly nothing has felt the same since. I go through the days kind of on autopilot, like I'm just going through the motions but nothing actually feels real or meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd at least try.
therapist: I'm so sorry for the loss of your dad — losing someone that suddenly, with no time to prepare, can leave you feeling completely unmoored, and what you're describing, that sense of going through the motions while the world feels unreal, is a very human response to profound grief. I notice there's something quiet and heavy in the way you're sharing this, almost like part of you is carrying more than the words quite capture. It means a lot that you decided to try, and I'd gently ask — when you say you're not sure talking will change anything, what would you most need it to do for you, even a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess if I'm being honest, I don't really know what I need. Part of me just wants to feel less like I'm floating through my own life, like something could actually feel solid again. But I also don't know if that's even possible right now, or if I'm just supposed to keep waiting for it to get better on its own.
therapist: That image of wanting something to feel solid again is really powerful, and it tells me you haven't given up — there's still a part of you reaching for something, even through all this fog. Grief doesn't follow a timeline, and waiting passively for it to lift on its own can sometimes leave us feeling even more powerless. I'm curious — are there any small moments, even brief ones, in these past two months where something did feel even slightly more real or present to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: There was this one moment maybe a few weeks ago where I was making coffee in the morning, the same way my dad used to make it, really strong with just a little milk, and for a second it felt like he was almost there. But then it hit me all over again that he wasn't, and it just made everything hurt more, so I'm not sure that counts as what you're asking about. It's like even the moments that feel real end up just reminding me of what I lost.
therapist: That absolutely counts — in fact, that moment with the coffee is really significant, because even through the pain, you were genuinely *present* for a few seconds, connected to him in a real way. It makes sense that it hurt so much afterward, but I wonder if those two things can exist together — that the moments which bring him closest are also the ones that remind you of the loss, and that's not a reason to avoid them, but maybe a sign of how much the love is still alive in you. What do you think your dad would have made of you carrying him with you in something as small and ordinary as the way you take your coffee?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: He probably would have laughed and said something like "at least you got the recipe right." He had this way of making things feel lighter without dismissing them, and thinking about that actually made me smile for a second just now, which feels weird because I also feel guilty about it. Like I'm not sure I'm allowed to smile when I'm still this sad about losing him.
therapist: That smile is not a betrayal — it's actually a beautiful sign that your dad's spirit is still reaching you, and it sounds like *he* would have been the first person to tell you that. The idea that we have to choose between grief and joy is one of the most common and painful myths about loss, but love doesn't work that way — you can miss him deeply and still let him make you smile, just like he always did. Where do you think that "rule" about not being allowed to smile came from for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think maybe it comes from feeling like if I'm okay even for a moment, it means I'm moving on, and moving on feels like forgetting him or like I didn't love him enough. There's also this thing where I feel like other people are watching, like my mom or my sister, and if they see me laughing they'll think I'm not taking the loss seriously. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it's really hard to shake.
therapist: It doesn't sound irrational at all — it sounds like you're carrying grief not just for your dad, but also a kind of watchfulness, making sure everyone around you knows how much he mattered. That belief that "being okay equals forgetting" is actually incredibly common in grief, but it's worth gently challenging — because your dad clearly knew how to hold love and lightness at the same time, and maybe that's something he was quietly teaching you all along. I'm wondering, if your mom or sister *did* see you smile at a memory of him, is it possible they might actually feel something closer to relief or even connection, rather than judgment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Maybe, but I honestly don't know because we've barely talked about him since the funeral. Everyone kind of went back to their lives and we just don't bring him up, which makes me feel even more alone with it, like I'm the only one still drowning while everyone else is somehow keeping their heads above water. I want to believe they'd feel connection instead of judgment, but the idea of being the one to bring him up and maybe making everyone cry or fall apart, that feels like too much responsibility right now.
therapist: That sense of being alone in the grief while life moves on around you is one of the loneliest feelings there is, and it makes so much sense that you're exhausted by the idea of being the one to break the silence. I want to gently reflect something back to you — you're describing carrying the weight of protecting everyone else from their own grief, almost like you've taken on the role of keeping the peace, even at the cost of your own need to not be so alone in this. What do you think would happen if you let yourself need something from your mom or sister, even just a small moment of remembering him together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think part of me is scared that if I bring him up, I'll see how much my mom is hurting and then I'll feel guilty for making it worse, even though I know logically she's already hurting whether I say anything or not. There's also this fear that maybe they've found a way to cope that I haven't, and if I crack that open it'll set everyone back. I want that connection but I don't know how to need something from people without feeling like a burden.
therapist: The logic you just named is so clear — you already know your mom is hurting whether you speak or not — and yet the heart doesn't always follow logic, especially when you've spent so long trying to protect the people you love. That feeling of being a burden is worth paying attention to, because it's quietly keeping you isolated from the very people who might be the only ones who truly understand what you've lost. I'm curious — do you think your dad ever felt like a burden to you when he needed something, or is that a rule you hold more for yourself than for the people you love?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: No, he never felt like a burden to me, not once, and I actually really valued the times he let me be there for him because it made me feel close to him. So I hear what you're saying, and I can see the double standard I'm applying to myself, but knowing that and actually believing I'm allowed to need people are two really different things. It's like I understand it in my head but I can't quite get it to land somewhere that actually changes how I feel.
therapist: You've just named one of the most important distinctions in this kind of work — that gap between understanding something and truly *feeling* it is real, and it's not a failure of yours, it's just where the deeper work lives. What strikes me is the tenderness in how you described those moments with your dad, how being needed by him actually brought you *closer* — and I wonder if somewhere in your body, in the quiet way you're holding all of this, part of you already knows you deserve that same closeness. What would it feel like, even just as an experiment, to let one person — your mom, your sister, anyone — be there for you the way you were there for your dad?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, just imagining it makes me feel kind of panicky, like there's this wall that goes up immediately. I think I'd want it to be my sister because she and my dad had this really specific bond that I think only she and I would understand, but I'm scared that if I reach out and she's not in a place to hold that, I'll feel even more alone than I do now. I guess the experiment idea makes sense in theory, but what if it doesn't go the way I'm hoping and it just confirms that I have to carry this by myself?
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — you're not really afraid of your sister, you're afraid of reaching out and discovering you're more alone than you hoped, and that's a vulnerable thing to risk. I notice you spoke about this quickly, like the words needed to come out before the wall fully went up, which tells me this matters deeply to you even as part of you wants to move past it. What if the goal of reaching out to your sister wasn't to have it go perfectly, but just to let her know you're carrying something and you thought of her — leaving the door open without putting everything on the line at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That framing actually feels a little less terrifying, like maybe I could send her a text that just says I was thinking about dad and thinking about her, without it having to turn into a whole conversation if she's not ready for that. But I'm still worried about what I do with myself in the time between sending it and hearing back, because that waiting space feels like it could be really painful. I think I'd spend the whole time convinced she's not going to respond, or that she will but in a way that feels distant, and I'm not sure I know how to sit with that uncertainty.
therapist: That small text idea is a really meaningful step, and the fact that it feels less terrifying tells me you're already finding a way to make this possible for yourself. The waiting space is hard, but it might be worth thinking about what you could do in that time to stay anchored — something that connects you to yourself, maybe even something small like that cup of coffee. What's one thing that has helped you feel even slightly more grounded on the harder days, something we could keep in your back pocket for exactly that kind of moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
